title: MC0-09444
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The principal appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and her minor children, associate appellants XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Nigeria. The principal appellant alleges that she fears being seriously harmed or persecuted in Nigeria by the chiefs of her husband's village who want to see him become the high priest. Since XXXX 2017, the village chiefs allegedly targeted the principal appellant to force her husband to accept the position. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, the principal appellant, her husband and their children reportedly left Nigeria together for the United States. The principal appellant and her children would later arrive in Canada. The associate appellants' refugee protection claims are based on that of their mother.
In an amendment made to her Basis of Claim Form, the principal appellant adds that she fears her now ex-husband because he had asked her to leave the children with a woman in the United States.
At the hearing, the principal appellant added that she feared her ex-husband would go after her and subject her to domestic violence since he is violent.

A representative of the Minister of Public Safety intervened in the matter and took part in the hearing before the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). She pointed out that the principal appellant gave contradictory testimony with respect to where her identity documents were located and she noted that the principal appellant uses three different names to identify herself.

On July 9, 2020, the RPD rejected the appellants' refugee protection claims because they had failed to credibly establish their identities. This is because the appellants' passports were not submitted into evidence and the principal appellant's explanations for the absence of these identity documents were not satisfactory, and also because of the numerous credibility issues noted in the identity documents submitted and in the principal appellant's testimony in this regard.

The appellants are appealing the RPD's decision as they are of the view that it erred in its assessment of the principal appellant's credibility by failing to consider her explanations and the documentary evidence submitted with respect to identity.
In this appeal, I am of the opinion that the determinative issue is whether the RPD erred in its analysis of the appellants' identities.

After conducting a full and independent analysis of the evidence provided, I am of the opinion that the appellants have failed to credibly establish their identities and that consequently, the RPD's decision is correct. Therefore, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I confirm the RPD's determination that the appellants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection." I dismiss the appeal.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) must apply the correctness standard of review in accordance with the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica.1 I will therefore conduct my own analysis of the record, including the transcripts of both sittings of the hearing, to determine whether the RPD erred.
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: The evidence presented by the person who is the subject of the appeal is only admissible if it meets the requirements set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. In other words, it is evidence that arose after the rejection of the claim, was not reasonably available, or that the person who is the subject of the appeal could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection of the refugee protection claim. If one of those conditions is met, the RAD will decide whether the evidence is credible, relevant and new in accordance with Singh2 and Raza.3

In this case, at the time of filing their appeal record, the appellants submitted the following documents: 1. A copy of passport No. XXXX issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant);4 2. A copy of passport No. XXXX issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2015, under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant);5 3. A copy of passport No. XXXX issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the associate appellant);6 4. A copy of passport No. XXXX issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the associate appellant);7 5. A copy of passport No. XXXX issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the associate appellant);8 6. Copy of an affidavit from XXXX XXXX XXXX concerning XXXX XXXX XXXX (the associate appellant) dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017;9 and 7. Copy of an affidavit from XXXX XXXX XXXX concerning XXXX XXXX XXXX (the associate appellant) dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017.10

The first four documents are copies of passports issued under the names of the appellants. In the principal appellant's case, I note that the passports were issued under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX, which differs from the name under which she arrived in Canada to claim refugee protection, namely XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. As for the last two documents-the affidavits-they are allegedly from the father of the minor associate appellants and state that he is their father and that the name XXXX is that of his grandfather.
I am of the opinion that these photocopies are not admissible into evidence since they do not meet any of the three requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

First, the six documents are dated before the RPD rejected the appellants' refugee protection claims on July 9, 2020, they were produced prior to this date and refer to a situation that had taken place even before the appellants left Nigeria. As a result, they do not meet the first criterion of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.11

Next, with respect to whether the six documents were not reasonably available, or that the principal appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time the refugee protection claim was rejected, I considered the explanations she provided in her affidavit.

The principal appellant argues therein that following the RPD's decision, she obtained access to copies of some of her and her children's identity documents. She explains that she had been unable to submit these documents since she did not have access to them as they were with her ex-husband, the father of her children, who was unaware that she was in Canada with them. She submits that she left the United States without notifying him since she was afraid that he would also come to Canada, that he was violent with her and that he wanted her to leave the children with a woman in the United States.

I am sensitive to the principal appellant's domestic violence allegations against her ex-husband, and I understand, as mentioned in Chairperson's Guideline 4:Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution, that women who make such allegations may require extremely sensitive handling. While I considered the principal appellant's explanations that she did not submit these documents out of fear for her ex-husband, I nevertheless find, for the following reasons, that her explanations are not satisfactory to credibly explain why these documents were not available to her at the time the RPD rejected her refugee protection claim.

As for the passports or their copies, I note that the principal appellant's explanation on appeal for failing to present these documents was the third version of what had allegedly happened. The evidence on the record, namely the detention review decision when she was detained for reasons of identity, shows that she explained to the immigration officer that she did not have the passports because she had forgotten them in a taxi on Roxham Road on the way to Canada.12 However, she testified at the hearing before the RPD that she had accidentally left her passport and those of her children in the United States, in the home of a man named XXXX whom she met at church. But she could not remember the name of the church or where it was located in New York State. Yet she states on appeal that she did not have them out of fear for her ex-husband.

Before the RPD, the principal appellant explained that there were two contradictory versions because she had always told the immigration officer the truth, and did not tell the officer that she had left her passports in a taxi. I have no reason to doubt the statement made by an immigration officer in the course of his duties, and who has no interest in the matter.

The principal appellant knew that proving her identity and that of her children was important, indeed crucial, in the processing of her refugee protection claim. She was questioned by the immigration officer about the absence of passports, she was detained for reasons of identity, and she had a detention review hearing on the matter before the Immigration Division. Most importantly, this matter was raised during the first sitting of the hearing before the RPD on October 16, 2019, just as it was during the second sitting on December 9, 2019. On all these occasions, the matter of establishing her identity and that of her children was raised, and the principal appellant was questioned about it and on her identity documents and those of her children, including the lack of passport evidence.

I must therefore conclude that the principal appellant had many opportunities to provide the explanation she offered on appeal, namely that she was unable to retrieve the documents earlier because her violent ex-husband had them and she feared revealing her location to him. Particularly before the RPD where she alleged at the hearing that she feared her ex-husband and mentioned that he held her passport for a certain period when they were all in Nigeria. What is more, seven months passed between the second sitting of the hearing and the RPD's decision, which gave her seven additional months to submit evidence to it to prove her identity and those of her children. In these circumstances, I do not accept the principal appellant's explanations for why these documents were not available at the time the appellants' refugee protection claims were rejected because they are not credible.

The onus was on the principal appellant to put her best case forward before the RPD before it rendered its decision. It should be noted that the role of the RAD is not to provide the opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD, but to allow for errors of fact, errors in law or mixed errors of fact and law to be corrected.13

In light of all the foregoing, I am of the opinion that the principal appellant failed to demonstrate that the six documents submitted into evidence were not reasonably available, or she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented to the RPD before their refugee protection claim was rejected on July 9, 2020.

Since the evidence does not meet any of the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, it is not necessary for me to examine whether they meet the case law criteria of credibility, relevance and newness from Singh14 and Raza.15 Furthermore, the evidence submitted is not admitted into evidence and there is no basis upon which the RAD may conduct an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

The RPD rejected the appellants' refugee protection claim because they did not credibly establish their identities. The appellants argue on appeal that the RPD erred in failing to consider the explanations and the documentary evidence submitted since many of the identity documents presented were rejected without considering the principal appellant's explanations.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: With all due respect for the appellants, I am of the opinion that the criticism is general and, most importantly, unfounded. This is because I note that the RPD conducted a lengthy and meticulous analysis of all of the evidence before it, including the principal appellant's various statements, identity documents submitted, and the documentary evidence on the record. It seems to me that the RPD was careful to point out to the principal appellant the problems observed in the evidence, that it had noted her explanations and provided reasons why it found them unsatisfactory and why it therefore decided not to give any weight to the documents submitted. The RPD then explained the impact of its findings on the principal appellant's credibility and on the establishment of her identity and those of her children. Consequently, the principal appellant's criticism against the RPD that it had disregarded the evidence and her explanations is unfounded.

This is all the more so because, based on my own analysis, I am of the opinion that the RPD's analysis and conclusions on this matter are correct for the following reasons. Absence of the appellants' passports

The RPD noted that the appellants' passports were not on the record. It considered the principal appellant's explanations, where she initially told the immigration officer that she had forgotten them in a taxi on Roxham Road on the way to Canada,16 and then testified at the RPD hearing that she had left them in the United States, in the home of a man named XXXX whom she had met in a church in New York State. She explained that she had consistently told the officer that the passports were not in a taxi. Yet this is a finding made by a federal public servant as part of his duties, and who had no interest in the case, and I do not see any reason to doubt its truthfulness. While the principal appellant provided a third version on appeal, stating that she was unable to submit them since they were with her ex-husband whom she fears, it should be noted that she did not share this with the RPD, even though she had told the RPD that she fears violence from her ex-husband when questioned on that topic, and she does not explain in her memorandum why she was unable to explain this to the RPD. The absence of the appellants' passports has deprived the RPD of valuable information concerning the appellants' identities and about their journey to come to Canada. In these circumstances and given that the principal appellant provided three contradictory versions to explain the absence of these documents, knowing that identity is a key factor of her and her children's refugee protection claims, I am of the opinion that these explanations are not satisfactory. In these circumstances, I find that the principal appellant's credibility is undermined, which has a negative impact on the establishment of the appellants' identities. The RPD did not err. Principal appellant's use of different names

The principal appellant submitted her refugee protection claim under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The RPD noted that the passport provided for her U.S. visa applications was issued under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX,17 although this name does not correspond to any of the names in the identity documents she submitted into evidence. On her birth certificate, certificate of origin and voter card, the name Blessing Amuwe Agebi appears instead, as on her emergency travel document, while her voter card is issued under the name of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and the name on her marriage certificate is XXXX XXXX.

The RPD questioned the principal appellant about the use of different names. She suggested an error in her marriage certificate, based on which her passport was issued. The error is as follows: at the bottom of the marriage certificate, one of the witnesses is referred to as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and that the XXXX in the witness's name corresponds to XXXX and that the XXXX in the witness's name should have been an XXXX XXXX which would have then corresponded to XXXX. She explained that it was her father-in-law who had included that name on her marriage certificate. The principal appellant later explained that XXXX XXXX is the name of her father-in-law's father, and that this name was recorded on the marriage certificate. I am of the opinion that this explanation is not satisfactory given that the names XXXXandXXXX XXXX do not appear on the marriage certificate issued by a church, and that her passport was not issued under her name as it appears on her marriage certificate. The principal appellant's credibility is undermined. The RPD did not err in drawing a negative inference from this situation.

The principal appellant also mentioned that a passport officer had told her that the last name in her passport should be the same as her husband's, which is XXXX. I find that this explanation is not credible since her husband's name on the marriage certificate is XXXX XXXX XXXX. The RPD also did not err in concluding that this explanation was not satisfactory.

The principal appellant explained before the RPD that different names were used simply because she had decided to change her name and she had stopped using XXXX XXXX after her father-in-law died in 2017. I find that this explanation is not credible since she did not take any formal steps in this regard and that consequently, she did not demonstrate that there was an actual name change to justify the authorities issuing identity documents under different names.

What is more, when she testified that she was unable to take formal steps to change her name because her passport was with her husband, the RPD told her that, according to the documentary evidence on the record, it was possible to use affidavits to make a name change in her country. The principal appellant testified that she did not want to change the name in her passport. This in no way explains the contradiction between her statements and the documentary evidence as to how a name change is made and the fact that she was unable to do it because her husband had her passport. This explanation does not demonstrate that any name change had been made with the Nigerian authorities. Even an informal change cannot explain why identity documents were issued under different names for the same person. In these circumstances, the principal appellant's testimony to explain that different names were used because of a name change is not credible. Her credibility is undermined.

The principal appellant submits on appeal that because the name on her marriage certificate includes XXXX, she used it to obtain the other identity documents, which would explain why they were issued under the name of XXXX. However, I note that on this church-issued marriage certificate, the name XXXX does not appear anywhere on it to identify her, her husband or the witnesses. Consequently, I find that the principal appellant's explanation is not credible, just as I find it not credible that the authorities had issued identity documents with the name XXXX XXXX based on a marriage certificate where the name also does not appear. The principal appellant's explanation is all the more lacking in credibility given that XXXX does not appear on her birth certificate, her certificate of origin or on her voter card. Consequently, rather than satisfactorily shedding light on the credibility issues noted by the RPD, the principal appellant's explanation on appeal actually highlighted these problems.

Finally, I should point out that I have considered the principal appellant's submissions that she has little education, that she has always followed men's orders, and that they were in charge of administrative matters. While I appreciate that the principal appellant relied on men, I note that she completed six years of secondary school and, particularly in light of the foregoing, it is clear that her explanations contradict the evidence and that the evidence contradicts itself. Moreover, there is much confusion in her explanations which, in my view, do not explain why different names were used in the identity documents she herself submitted into evidence to establish her identity. She bears the burden of proof. In these circumstances, the RPD did not err in drawing a negative inference from the use of different names on the identity documents submitted by the principal appellant. Analysis of each of the appellants' identity documents

Despite the seriousness of the issues noted so far, the RPD took the time to analyze each of the identity documents the appellants provided, including the principal appellant's voter card, her birth certificate, her certificate of origin, her emergency travel certificate, her marriage certificate, her transcripts and other academic documents, as well as the minor appellants' birth certificates. The RPD noted the problems and discrepancies observed in the documents, the principal appellant's explanations and its assessment of these explanations. The RPD then explained the impact of its own findings on the principal appellant's credibility and on the establishment of the appellants' identities. In this context, I am once again of the view that the RPD in no way disregarded the documents submitted in evidence or the principal appellant's explanations. Given that the passports were not on the record, the RPD had no choice but to examine the identity documents that were submitted to it in evidence, and this is not an increased attention to detail or formality as the appellants suggested, but rather a comprehensive review of the evidence. That is what needed to be done.

I also note that in addition to the general criticism I have just addressed and that regarding the principal appellant's marriage certificate and passport, the appellants did not raise any specific errors allegedly made by the RPD in reviewing each of the identity documents listed above or the minor associate appellants' birth certificates, and which revealed numerous and significant irregularities. Based on my own review, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err in its analysis or in its conclusions pertaining to these documents. Voter card

As for the principal appellant's voter card, it can be noted that it does not include the features normally found on this document, as reported in the documentary evidence on Nigeria.18 For instance, the name of the state the voter is registered in is not listed. The principal appellant explained that this was because the information is part of the government's record. I find that it is not credible that the government, namely the authority that issues voter cards, would refrain from including information which, according to its own guidelines, should be there because it already has this information in its records. In these circumstances, I agree with the RPD that this discrepancy undermines the probative value of this document.

What is more, the documentary evidence reports that voter cards have many components and specialized features (e.g. base substrate, security printing, personalization, lamination and chip embedding), and that it is designed with an average life span of ten (10) years. It also reports that the card has an embedded chip that contains all the biometrics of a legitimate holder (including fingerprints and facial image) and that it has security features that are not easily susceptible to counterfeiting. However, the Minister analyzed the principal appellant's voter card and, according to the expert report, her card has none of security features to verify its authenticity, and the printing techniques used can be done by a commercial enterprise and, consequently, illegitimate production is highly possible.19 The principal appellant did not provide any explanation about these issues regarding the features of her voter card. In light of the scope of the problems noted on the voter card, I am of the opinion that the RPD was correct in not giving any probative value to this document to establish the principal appellant's identity. Birth certificate

The principal appellant claimed that she had asked her father to obtain her birth certificate because some friends had told her that she looked small for her age, and that she had obtained it by going to an office with her father. However, she was unable to state what type of office it was, and when the RPD had asked her, she could not explain which documents were submitted to obtain her birth certificate. Yet the principal appellant was a 24-year-old adult when she undertook this process with her father. In this context, her inability to state where she had obtained the certificate and on the basis of which documents the certificate was issued on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2005, 24 years after she was born on XXXX XXXX, 1980, undermines her credibility. What is more, it appears from the submissions and conclusions of the expert report for the examination of authenticity of the birth certificate that it was a potentially counterfeit apocryphal document.20 In these circumstances and in light of the foregoing regarding the principal appellant's inability to state which office she visited to obtain the birth certificate and what she had to provide to obtain it, I am of the opinion that this document has no probative value to establish the principal appellant's identity. The RPD did not err. Certificate of origin

According to the documentary evidence, this document is used to prove her Nigerian origin and it is required to obtain a passport. This document is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2007.21 The principal appellant explained that she did not know when she had obtained it, but that it was during the time she had gone before the court to have her name changed, and she was asked for it then because she had failed to bring her passport.22 However, it should be noted that based on her claims, it was actually a decade later in 2017 that she tried to change her name, which contradicts her earlier statement. When asked to explain, she contradicted herself even more by explaining that she had it well before she had taken steps to change her name. In these circumstances, and in light of the significant credibility issues regarding a name change, I am of the opinion that this response does not explain her contradictory versions with respect to obtaining this document. What is more, it should be noted that the certificate does not include the principal appellant's photograph, biometrics or special security features, and that the name on the certificate of origin does not correspond to the name the principal appellant allegedly used on her passport. The RPD noted other problems in the principal appellant's testimony regarding this document, but I am of the opinion that the problems raised so far are sufficient to not give any probative value to this document to establish the principal appellant's identity. The RPD did not err in its conclusion. Emergency travel certificate

The principal appellant claims that she obtained this document by applying online with the Nigerian High Commission in Ottawa, which sent it to her after she submitted her voter card, birth certificate and certificate of origin by email. She stated that she did not show an airline ticket. Yet the way in which she obtained the document does not correspond with the procedure described by the Nigerian High Commission in Ottawa in the documentary evidence.23 The principal appellant did not submit, as required, a police report or a copy of the bio-data page of her Nigerian Passport, which she did not have, nor did she have her airline ticket. What is more, it should be noted that she allegedly obtained this emergency travel certificate based on documents in which numerous issues were noted, including a birth certificate that the expert report concluded was apocryphal after review. In these circumstances, I am of the opinion that this document does not have any probative value to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the principal appellant's identity. The RPD did not err. Marriage certificate and education documents

With respect to the marriage certificate, based on the analysis carried out above outlining numerous problems and discrepancies, it cannot establish the principal appellant's identity on a balance of probabilities. The RPD did not err in its conclusion in this regard.

As for the education documents, transcripts, diploma and primary and secondary education certificates, they do not have security features, nor do they include the principal appellant's photograph or biometrics. Her complete date of birth is not indicated on her primary education certificate and her guardian is simply identified as "Egege." What is more, each of these documents was issued under a different name, which differs from the name she uses in her refugee protection claim. In these circumstances, I am of the opinion that the academic documents are not sufficient to establish the principal appellant's identity on a balance of probabilities. The RPD did not err. Children's birth certificates

While the appellants did not raise any specific errors in the examination of the children's birth certificates, based on my own analysis, I note that the father's name is different for each child. The principal appellant explained that this was because a person can have up to three names in Nigeria. I am of the view that this does not explain why the father's name is different for each child when they have one and the same father, the ex-husband. I also note that none of the names used in the minor associate appellants' birth certificates to designate their father, who is allegedly their mother's husband, are consistent with the name indicated on their marriage certificate. In addition, the name of the mother-the principal appellant-which is also on the minor appellants' birth certificates, differs by certificate and differs from the names used in her identity documents. In these circumstances, these problems further undermine the principal appellant's credibility regarding the establishment of her identity and those of her children.

Lastly, I should add that I considered the fact that the principal appellant may have been nervous and shy during her hearing, that some individuals can have a slower pace and that she has a secondary education.24 However, as shown in the analysis above, these personal considerations cannot explain the numerous problems noted in the identity documents submitted, including discrepancies, the absence of passports, and her use of different names to identify herself.

Similarly, if the identity documents submitted are from Nigeria and, as the appellants noted on appeal, if it were accepted that this involves an African country where customs and government organizations do not operate as they do in Canada, I am of the view that this does not explain the multiple problems and discrepancies noted by the RPD, and the contradictions and inconsistencies in the principal appellant's testimony in this regard.

In light of all the foregoing, I am of the opinion that the appellants failed to establish their identities on a balance of probabilities. Consequently, I am of the view that the RPD's decision that the appellants failed to discharge their burden of proof with regard to establishing that there is a serious possibility that they will be persecuted on a Convention ground or that they will be subjected personally to a danger of torture or to a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they returned to Nigeria is correct.

After analyzing all of the evidence on the record, the panel determines that the appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection."
